abstract:
We introduce a family of diagrammatical equational theories unifying two research programs: categorical quantum mechanics and graphical linear algebra. We prove their completeness with respect to denotational semantics described in terms of relations between vector spaces equipped with symplectic structure. This provides versatile graphical languages encompassing both affinely constrained classical mechanical systems, as well as odd-prime-dimensional stabiliser and Gaussian quantum circuits. Terms are described by labelled graphs with input and output interfaces, and the languages are equipped with equational theories amenable to standard graph rewriting techniques.
In order to reason about large composite systems, we introduce a compact scalable notation where the vertices are themselves labelled by graphs. This notation allows us to state new and powerful rewrite rules which operate on diagrams at a large scale. We also show how this notation neatly captures some important constructions, such as graph states of quantum computing and the impedance and admittance matrices of electrical networks.

 1      Introduction
A common approach to giving semantics to a computational process is to specify it as a
relation between inputs and outputs describing the admissible behaviors of the system [60].
Diagrammatic languages provide a particularly effective syntax for reasoning about such
relational semantics, as they admit equational theories that can be manipulated using graph
rewriting and normalisation techniques.
    In this work, we introduce a family of diagrammatic equational theories whose denotational
semantics is given by linear relations between symplectic vector spaces (i.e. Lagrangian
relations). These theories admit a sound and complete graphical calculus, allowing equational

         The ZX-calculus is a family of diagrammatic languages for representing and reasoning
      about quantum processes [29, 54], where diagrams represent linear maps between finite-
      dimensional systems. For example, the following diagrammatic derivation establishes the

      The ZX-calculus has been applied to an increasing variety of problems in the field of
      quantum computation, such as circuit optimisation [31, 42], cross-compilation [4, 58], error
      correction [7, 24, 32, 33], classical simulation [43, 44] and many more [1]. In parallel, the
      programme of Graphical Algebra develops diagrammatic presentations for concrete algebraic
      structures, such as linear maps and relations [8, 11, 13, 15, 53]. These languages are also
      equipped with equational theories amenable to rewriting, and have been used to interpret
      diverse models, such as electrical circuits [9,13], Petri nets [12], and probabilistic programs [53].
         Several connections between these two research programs have been remarked upon
      in the literature. Notably, the phase-free fragment of the ZX-calculus is equivalent to
      Graphical Linear Algebra over the finite field F2 [16, 41]. Moreover, it is known that the
      stabiliser fragment of quantum theory in any odd-prime dimension p can be interpreted within
      Graphical Affine Algebra over the finite field Fp , yielding a stabiliser ZX-calculus for odd
      prime dimensions [30]. These results suggest the existence of a more general diagrammatic
      theory underlying both approaches.
          In this paper, we introduce Graphical Symplectic Algebra (GSA), a family of diagrammatic
      equational theories parametrised by a field, whose semantics is given by Lagrangian relations.
      GSA generalises odd-prime-dimensional stabiliser ZX-calculi [17, 49], while extending their
      scope to a broader class of linear-algebraic and relational models. Our main technical result
      is a completeness theorem via a normal form: every semantic equality between Lagrangian
      relations is derivable using the graphical rewrite rules of the calculus.
          A key contribution of this article is the introduction of a scalable diagrammatic notation
      for GSA, designed for reasoning about operations on large composite systems. In this
      notation, certain structured families of diagrams can be internalised as labels of vertices,
      yielding higher-level rewrite rules that operate uniformly over arbitrarily large systems.
      This generalises the scalable ZX-calculus of Carette et al. [23], and enables a synthetic
      completeness proof that avoids the combinatorial overhead common in existing diagrammatic
      arguments [49].
         Finally, we show how the expressive power of GSA encompasses a range of important
      examples. Depending on the chosen interpretation, diagrams can represent stabiliser and
      Gaussian quantum circuits, affinely constrained classical systems, quantum graph states [45],
      and network-theoretic constructions such as impedance and admittance matrices [48].



      Outline. In Sections 2 and 3 we review string diagrams and Graphical Affine Algebra. We
      introduce Graphical Symplectic Algebra in Section 4, followed by its scalable notation in
      Section 5, and normal form in Section 6. Proofs are left to appendices.

Flexsymmetry
Many graphical calculi (e.g. ZX- and ZH-calculus, Graphical Linear Algebra) admit presenta-
tions in which only the connectivity of diagrams matters: boxes do not distinguish the order
of their input or output wires. This property is presentation-dependent, so to ensure it holds
in our setting, we impose the following condition on (some) generators:

▶ Definition 2 (Carette [22]). A generator g : m → n is flexsymmetric if it is invariant
under any permutation of its wires, where permutations are built from the symmetry and
(when necessary) the compact structure. Diagrammatically, this amounts to

for any permutation σ : n + m → n + m implemented using the symmetry.

Flexsymmetry guarantees that the order of a generator’s wires is irrelevant, so diagrams can

          4        Graphical Symplectic Algebra
      Many physical systems – quantum, mechanical, electrical – are governed by pairs of conjugate
      quantities (position–momentum [2, 56], voltage–current [6], Z–X [35], etc), leading to state
      spaces naturally equipped with a symplectic form. The admissible transformations of such
      systems, i.e. those that preserve the symplectic form and are restricted to linear or affine
      processes, correspond to Lagrangian relations [57]. This motivates our choice of denotational
      semantics. We briefly recall the relevant definitions before introducing our calculus.

      symplectic form. By a standard result due to Darboux, in finite dimensions, all such spaces
      are isomorphic to ones of the following form:

       We have given a sound, universal and complete graphical language for affine Lagrangian
       relations, and shown how this gives a syntax for classes of both quantum and classical
       circuits. Using the scalable notation, we have given a high-level tool for reasoning about
       large mechanical networks, and unified the graphical treatments of local complementation
       and pivoting for quantum graph states with the star-mesh identities for electrical circuits
       using Schur complementation. These ideas have already led to significant progress, yielding
       the first complete calculus for infinite-dimensional quantum mechanics [18].
           It is future work to refine the syntax of GASAF to represent more restrictive physical
       semantics, where extra structure must be preserved; possibly more firmly connecting our work
       with other graphical treatments of electrical circuits [9, 28]. Conversely, it is also interesting
       to generalise our work to nonlinear (nonaffine) settings of physical interest. The category of
       affine Lagrangian relations has also been used as the foundation for a denotational semantics
       for stabiliser quantum programs [20]: it is a natural future direction to explore a graphical
       presentation of those semantics via GASAF .
